newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb army calls for end to political rift.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb army calls for end to political rift.

text.p: The Bosnian Serb army issued a cautious statement on Wednesday calling for a legal solution to a power struggle between the president and hardliners loyal to indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.
The statement was issued by the army general staff after a 90-minute meeting with embattled President Biljana Plavsic in her offices in the northern town of Banja Luka.
It stopped short of an outright endorsement of Plavsic but said the conflict should be resolved within political institutions as soon as possible.
It also said the army would "stay within the law and preserve its legitimacy while respecting the competencies of the president."

General Pero Colic, commander of the army, and other senior officers are believed to back Plavsic but analysts said the statement indicated the military was hesitant to threaten to interve in the crisis.
In a sign the army was uncertain about the loyalties of its own officers, the general staff demanded adherence to a "single chain of command" and said that "all orders must go via the general staff."

The power struggle between Plavsic and Karadzic, who was forced to step down as president last year because of his status as a suspect named by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, erupted into the open this year.
The army's response carried important symbolism but Karadzic and his allies control a large, heavily-armed police force which has become more powerful than the military in peacetime.
The army, recently purged by Karadzic, lacks financial support and its movements are severely restricted under rules enforced by a NATO-led peacekeeping force.

Karadzic's media has accused NATO of protecting Plavsic and interfering in the feud. Plavsic has vehemently denied this and NATO says it has merely deployed additional troops to "maintain a secure environment" around Banja Luka.
Countering such charges from hardliners, the general staff said all contact with NATO regarding Plavsic's security arrangements "must be broken off."

A police commander considered loyal to Plavsic told independent radio B-92 in Belgrade that her security unit became concerned when it received a report on Tuesday that the Interior Ministry was preparing a crackdown on policemen siding with Plavsic.
The officer said a group of 60 policemen sent to Banja Luka eventually withdrew from the town.

A NATO spokesman told reporters that the Stabilisation Force stepped up patrols in Banja Luka on Tuesday night due to indications of a "threat to security." He declined to elaborate on the nature of the threat.
